The iPad mini doesn’t even have affordability to recommend it these days, starting at a scarcely budget-friendly $599. The cheap option is the standard iPad at $449, and that comes with a bigger display.
Today’s challenge will be to make the iPad mini relevant again. An OLED screen is a nice idea, but is it enough to shift perceptions of a product that faces superior alternatives in every direction? title: iPad mini (A20 Pro): Apple’s smallest tablet is suddenly its biggest upgrade
content:
Macworld





On October 26, Apple unveiled the next iPad mini with an OLED display, a faster A20 Pro chip, and more. Customers can pre-order the device on October 28, with shipments starting on November 6.
The new iPad mini replaced a model that was released in 2024. That model had an A17 Pro chip, an 8.3-inch display, and a thicker design. Here is everything you need to know about the 2026 iPad mini.
iPad mini (A17 Pro) and iPad mini (A20 Pro) compared


iPad mini (A17 Pro)iPad mini (A20 Pro)

Display8.3-inch Liquid Retina LCD display8.5-inch Super Retina OLED display
ProcessorA17 Pro (8GB RAM)A20 Pro (12GB RAM)
Storage128/256/512GB128/256/512GB
Front camera12MP Center Stage camera12MP Landscape Center Stage camera
Rear camera12MP Wide camera12MP Wide camera
BiometricsTouch ID in top buttonTouch ID in top button
AudioLandscape stereo speakersAcoustic Display
ColorsSpace Gray, Blue, Purple, StarlightMidnight, Starlight
DimensionsH: 7.69 inches (195.4 mm)
W: 5.3 inches (134.8 mm)
D: 0.25 inch (6.3 mm)H: 7.69 inches (195.3 mm)
W: 5.22 inches (132.6 mm)
D: 0.21 inch (5.4 mm)
Weight0.65 pound (293 grams)0.56 pound (255 grams)
Price$599$699

 



iPad mini (A20 Pro): Performance and specs 
A20 Pro
C2 modem in cellular models
N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread
The new iPad mini makes a much bigger processor jump than previously expected. It features an A20 Pro chip, which was introduced with the iPhone 18 Pro in September. However, Apple offers different versions of the A20 Pro in the mini, depending on how much storage you get. Here are the differences.


128GB or 256GB512GB

CPU5-core CPU: 2 super cores and 3 efficiency cores6-core CPU: 2 super cores and 4 efficiency cores
GPU7-core GPU7-core GPU
Neural Engine16-core Neural EngineDual 16-core Neural Engine

 



Moving from the A17 Pro to the A20 Pro represents a major performance upgrade. The new chip brings substantially faster CPU and graphics performance, along with more capable on-device AI processing for Apple Intelligence, gaming, photo editing and other demanding workloads. It also makes the iPad mini unusually powerful for its size and narrows the performance gap with Apple’s larger iPads. Also with the upgrade to the A20 Pro, the iPad mini now has 12GB of RAM; the A17 Pro iPad mini had 8GB.
The N1 networking chip adds support for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread. Cellular connectivity is provided by Apple’s C2 modem, which replaces the Qualcomm modem used in the A17 Pro iPad mini. Cellular connectivity is an option that adds $150/£150 to the price.







iPad mini (A20 Pro): Display
OLED Super Retina tech
8.5 inches

				
					

				
			
Apple




With the A20 Pro iPad mini, Apple upgraded the display from 8.3 inches to 8,5 inches and from LCD to OLED, making the mini the second tablet with the tech. OLED (which Apple markets as Super Retina XDR) brings deeper blacks, higher contrast, faster pixel response, and improved viewing angles compared with the Liquid Reitina LCD in the current iPad mini.
While both screens are classified as Super Retina, however, the iPad mini does not have the same display technology as the iPad Pro. Apple uses a single-stack LTPS OLED panel, rather than the tandem OLED and LTPO technology used in the Pro models. This keeps costs lower, but the single panel does not reach the same brightness levels as the iPad Pro display (1,600 vs 1,200).
Another difference between the OLEDs in the iPad mini and iPad Pro is ProMotion. That means that the maximum refresh rate in the iPad mini is 60Hz. The iPad Pro has ProMotion that supports up to 120Hz refresh for speedy scrolling and smoother animations.
WIth the 256GB and 512GB models, Apple offers a nano-texture display glass option, which provides a matte-like display instead of glossy. The nano-texture option is an additional $100/£100.



						

							


2026 iPad mini: Design
Thinner and lighter
Improved water- and dust-resistance
New vibration-based speaker system

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPad mini has retained the same overall design since its major redesign in 2021. However, the A20 Pro iPad mini is thinner than its predecessor, measuring 0.21 inches (5.4 mm) compared to 0.25 inches (6.3 mm). Its width is 5.22 inches (132.6 mm), which is slightly narrower than the 5.3 inches (134.8 mm) or the older iPad mini. The iPad mini (A20 Pro) weighs 0.56 pounds (255 grams), quite a bit lighter than the older model’s 0.65 pounds (293 grams).




Tthe iPad mini (A20 Pro) is more water- and dust-resistant than before, with an IP67 rating. As part of this, Apple introduced a new Acoustic Display in the iPad mini, where specially designed woofers are paired through the display, and custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminium enclosure.
With the iPad mini, (A20 Pro), Apple decide to narrow the color choices to Midnight and Starlight. The previous iPad mini was available in Blue, Purple, Starlight, and Space Gray, 


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Cameras 
Landscape front camera
No major camera sensor upgrades

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPad mini’s 12MP FaceTime camera moves from the short edge to the more convenient landscape edge. It also gets a larger ƒ/2.0 aperture, up from ƒ/2.4.
As for the rear camera the specs are the same as before: a 12MP Wide camera with an ƒ/1.8 aperture, 5x digital zoom, adaptive True Tone flash, Smart HDR 4 for photos, 4K video recording at 24 fps, 25 fps, 30 fps, or 60 fps, and 3x video zoom. The A20 Pro chip could still improve image processing and computational photography.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Price 
The iPad mini (A20 Pro) starts at $699/£699. That’s a $100/£100 increase over the iPad mini (A17 Pro), which had its price increased in June 2026 from its initial $499/£499 starting price. Storage options cost an extra $100 per 128GB, so $100 extra for 256GB ($799) and $300 more for 512GB ($999).

title: Quickly Silence iPhone Duo Without a Ring/Mute Switch
content:
The new iPhone Duo drops both the classic Ring/Silent switch as well as the newer Action button, so there is no physical mute control on the device, and no way to assign the Silent Mode control to another button. That said, you can still silence the device pretty quickly – you just do it on-screen instead using a new way to invoke Control Center.


With your device unlocked, open Control Center by tapping the circular "status bar" icon, then tap the Silent Mode button (the bell icon). That's all there is to it. 

Settings ➝ Sounds & Haptics ➝ Show in Status Bar. 

How to Add Silent Mode to Control Center

Silent Mode is included in the default set of controls at the top of the Control Center, but if you don't see it, you can add it manually by following these steps:
Tap the circular status bar icon to open Control Center.

Tap the plus (+) icon in the top-left corner, then tap Add a Control at the bottom of the screen.

Scroll down to the Sounds section or use the search bar to find it, then select Silent Mode.

title: The iPad mini just got thinner, lighter, and surprisingly powerful
content:
Macworld





As part of what it expected to be three days of announcements, Apple today unveiled a new version of its iPad mini tablet, with the 8th-gen model boasting a slight redesign and major upgrades to its screen and processor.
Described by the company as “the most capable and versatile iPad mini ever,” the product runs an A20 Pro chip, a three-generation upgrade on the 2024 mini’s A17 Pro chip. Apple is pushing this as an important boost to the tablet’s power, claiming the new chip “supercharges AI.” The chip comes in two options. The 128GB and 256GB models get a 5-core CPU and a 16-core Neural Engine while the 512GB model, which costs $300 more than the 128GB model, gets the full 6-core chip with a dual 16-core Neural Engine. 
Unlike the first six models in the series, which were labelled by generation, the last two have been explicitly defined on Apple’s website by their chip–so this is officially the “iPad mini (A20 Pro).”
With the exception of the very expensive Pro models at the top of the range, iPads in general tend to be bought by customers more interested in consuming media than churning through difficult processing tasks. The chip upgrade is therefore more a matter of future-proofing the new mini to be able to manage everyday tasks several years from now. iPad owners, to Apple’s chagrin, tend to hold on to them for a long time.
Those casual users may be prompted to make an early upgrade by similarly major upgrades to the mini’s screen. Movies and TV shows should look better on this hardware, which is slightly larger as well as promising substantially better picture quality.
The A17 Pro iPad mini had an 8.3-inch “Liquid Retina” LED screen with a resolution of 2266 x 1488 and a maximum brightness of 500 nits. The A20 Pro mode improves on those specs in every way, coming in at 8.5 inches, a “Super Retina XDR” branding, OLED technology, and a resolution of 2316 x 1512 (that’s the same sharpness, just covering a larger area). As for brightness, the new mini is capable of a maximum standard brightness of 600 nits, and can go all the way up to 1,200 nits peak brightness on HDR content.
OLED is the headline upgrade there. The technology delivers deeper blacks than LED, richer and crisper colors, and better handling of HDR content. On top of that, the new mini brings the option to add nano-texture glass to the display, something which was previously restricted (at least in Apple’s tablet range) to the iPad Pro. It isn’t offered on the current iPad Air or standard iPad. it’s only available on the 256GB and 512GB models, and costs an additional $100.
Aside from the chip and screen, the mini’s third major upgrade is its design. Despite the inclusion of a larger screen its length and width are virtually identical to the previous model (they’ve actually shrunk a tiny bit, from 195.4 x 134.8 mm to 195.3 x 132.6 mm), but the device is a lot thinner (from 6.3 mm down to 5.4 mm) and significantly lighter (from 0.65 pounds/293g down to 0.56 pounds/255g). In a nutshell, the mini is now more portable than ever.
Those are the big three changes. But there are other upgrades: actual dust and water resistance (it gets a very high IP67 rating); the FaceTime camera moves from the short to the more convenient landscape edge (and also gets a larger f/2.0 aperture, up from f/2.4); Wi-Fi moves from version 6e to 7; Bluetooth from 5.3 to 6; and the speakers are upgraded to what Apple descries as an “Acoustic Display.” (“Specially designed woofers are paired through the display to produce punchier bass and more volume,” the company explains, while “custom tweeters are now hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure for clearer highs.”) The device is also rated for fast charging: Apple claims you can charge up to 50 percent in 30 minutes with compatible charging equipment.
The new iPad mini starts at $699/£699 for the Wi-Fi model, or $849/£849 for the cellular one. Preorders start on Wednesday, October 28, and the device will hit stores on Friday, November 6.

title: New iPad mini shrinks just enough to complicate case compatibility
content:
Apple's new iPad mini has slimmed down with a thinner, narrower design, but those minor changes could make your perfectly good old case a lousy fit.

iPad mini 7
The OLED upgrade increases the display size from 8.3 inches to 8.5 inches while keeping roughly the same footprint. However, Apple's published measurements reveal several physical differences that could affect case compatibility.
The sixth-generation iPad mini from 2021 and the A17 Pro model from 2024 have identical dimensions of 195.4 mm tall, 134.8 mm wide, and 6.3 mm thick.
The 2026 model measures 195.3 mm tall, 132.6 mm wide, and 5.4 mm thick, according to Apple's technical specifications. The height difference is just 0.1 mm, but the reductions in width and thickness could affect how older cases grip the device.

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro: OLED, design and release date rumors
content:
Macworld





Apple could be just days away from unveiling its first touchscreen MacBook Pro. The company is holding a media event on October 28, 2026, when it is expected to reveal the first touchscreen MacBook Pro as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout. If the rumors are accurate, this could be one of the biggest changes to the MacBook Pro in its history.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way.
The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrated its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
The redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to be a premium model featuring M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, rather than the newer M6 chip. Apple is separately preparing a standard 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro, which is expected to retain the existing design. For more on that model, see our M6 MacBook Pro release date and specs guide.
There are still questions over pricing and availability. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures could make the touchscreen models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro, while touch support is expected to remain exclusive to Apple’s premium laptops initially. Read on for everything we know about the touchscreen MacBook Pro’s expected release date, design, specifications and price, including what Apple could announce on October 28.


Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
Apple media experience confirmed for October 28; touchscreen MacBook Pro announcement expected
On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. This is expected to be the introduction of new Macs, including the touchscreen MacBook Pro.


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026





Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 25 that Apple will reveal the touchscreen MacBook Pro on Wednesday, October 28. Gurman has previously reported on October 8 that Apple plans to announce its first touchscreen MacBook on October 27. The launch will reportedly include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press on October 28. In his Power On podcast, Gurman said the laptop will start shipping on November 6.
Earlier reports offered a broader launch window and raised the possibility of delays. Speaking in a Power On podcast on October 1, Gurman said he expected the touchscreen MacBook announcement as early as October, potentially slipping to November. The laptops are reportedly being tested with macOS 27.2.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.
Gurman’s more recent reporting points to an October announcement and November availability. However, the launch was previously predicted for early 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule. 


						

							


Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen? 
Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips
Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.
Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.
For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.
The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design
Lighter design expected
Punch hole for the FaceTime camera

				
					

				
			The last time Apple included touch with the MacBook was the TouchBar, which was a flop. But this time could it work out better for Apple? 
Foundry




Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to have a substantially lighter design than current models, but it may not be significantly thinner. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has revised his earlier expectations for a slimmer body while maintaining that Apple has redesigned and consolidated internal components to reduce weight. 
One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.
Other rumoured design changes include:
A lighter chassis, although the latest reporting suggests it may not be thinner.
OLED display technology.
A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.
These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.


						

							


Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?
M5 Pro and M5 Max
Early rumors suggested that Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro would feature M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but more recent reports indicate that Apple has changed its plans. The redesigned OLED models are now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, with Apple potentially skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation entirely.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple has revised its chip roadmap to accelerate development of the AI-focused M7 generation. The change could bring the M7 chips to market around six months earlier, with significantly improved on-device AI capabilities. The ongoing DRAM and NAND shortages may also have influenced Apple’s decision, although they are not thought to be the primary reason. Apple has already increased Mac and iPad prices in response to rising memory costs. Read more about Apple’s reported chip roadmap changes.
Separately, Apple is reportedly planning to launch the 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip.
There has also been speculation that Apple could introduce its own 5G modem to a future MacBook Pro, enabling cellular connectivity without Wi-Fi or an iPhone hotspot. However, there is little concrete evidence that cellular connectivity will be part of the touchscreen redesign.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Display
Tandem OLED display
Touchscreen interface
The display is expected to be the headline upgrade of Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro. Multiple reports suggest Apple will replace the current Liquid Retina XDR (mini-LED) panel with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing MacBook Pro technology closer to the Ultra Retina XDR display used in the latest iPad Pro.
According to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, Apple is planning to introduce OLED touch panels in the MacBook Pro in late 2026 or early 2027. The new display is expected to be thinner, more power-efficient, and capable of delivering deeper blacks, higher contrast, richer colours, and improved HDR performance than today’s mini-LED screens.
Reports indicate that both the 14-inch and 16-inch models will use advanced tandem OLED technology, which combines two OLED layers to achieve higher brightness levels while maintaining excellent energy efficiency. Apple first introduced this technology with the M4 iPad Pro and is expected to bring a similar implementation to the MacBook Pro.
The touchscreen functionality will reportedly rely on on-cell touch technology, which integrates touch sensors directly into the display rather than adding a separate layer. This approach helps keep the panel thin while supporting multi-touch input.
If the rumours prove accurate, the move to a tandem OLED touchscreen would represent the biggest display upgrade in the MacBook Pro’s history and one of the most significant changes to the lineup in years.

				
					

				
			The iPad Pro has a tandem OLED display, the type of display that could make its way into the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Brady Snyder / Foundry



							


Touchscreen MacBook Interface 

				
					

				
			macOS 27 could have some hidden touchscreen features. 

Foundry




Apple is not expected to turn macOS into iPadOS, but reports suggest macOS 27 could include subtle design changes to make the Mac easier to use with touch input.
Rather than replacing the traditional desktop experience, Apple is reportedly working on a touch-tuned interface that adapts depending on how the device is being used. When touch input is detected, interface elements such as menus, buttons, and controls may automatically enlarge to make them easier to tap. When using a mouse or trackpad, macOS would revert to its familiar point-and-click layout.
The touchscreen itself is expected to support standard gestures such as tapping, scrolling, and zooming, while still allowing users to switch between touch, trackpad, and mouse input.
Further clues appeared in the macOS 27.2 beta on October 5. MacRumors reported new code references to touch gestures in Safari, Photos, Notes and Quick Look. These could support a future touchscreen MacBook, but they could also relate to Sidecar, which allows an iPad to act as a Mac display. 
More specific clues appeared in footage shared by itspdfu on October 14. The footage reportedly shows touch-oriented behavior in Safari in macOS 27.2 betas 3 and 4: tabs lift and enlarge while being rearranged, then return to their normal size when dropped into place. Pressing and holding a tab opens a contextual menu that omits the Ask Siri option available with a mouse or trackpad. These changes suggest Apple is preparing Safari for touch input.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Connectivity 
5G connectivity could finally come to the Mac

				
					

				
			The C1X is now available, but the C2 modem could arrive with the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Apple




Beyond the touchscreen display and redesigned chassis, one of the most intriguing rumours surrounding the next-generation MacBook Pro is built-in cellular connectivity.
Apple has spent the past several years developing its own modem technology, beginning with the C-series modem family. Reports suggest the company has explored bringing 5G connectivity to the MacBook lineup, allowing users to connect directly to mobile networks without relying on Wi-Fi or a smartphone hotspot.
In August 2025, Macworld reported that internal Apple code referenced a MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro chip and Apple’s C1 modem. This suggests Apple has experimented with cellular-equipped MacBooks, althogugh it does not establish that the upcoming touchscreen models will offer 5G.
The redesigned MacBook Pro could also benefit from Apple’s growing portfolio of wireless chips. The company’s N-series networking processors, which handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity, may eventually replace third-party components throughout the Mac lineup. An updated version of the chip could debut alongside the touchscreen MacBook Pro, improving power efficiency and tighter integration with Apple’s ecosystem.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Price expectations
Apple will likely offer similar configurations to the current MacBook Pro models, but it’s unclear how much of a premium a touchscreen OLED display will command. Apple upped the price of the iPad Pro by $200 when it got a tandem OLED, so it’s likely the touchscreen MacBook Pro will have a higher starting price.
Here are the prices for the current standard configurations of the M5 MacBook Pro, which saw prices increase between $300 and $500 in June 2026.
14-inch MacBook Pro
$1,999/£1,999: M5 with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 4
$2,499/£2,499: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,099/£4,099: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
16-inch MacBook Pro
$2,999/£2,999: M5 Pro with a 18-core CPU and 20-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,399/£4,399: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Everything we know about Apple’s next laptop
content:
Macworld





Apple is expected to launch a new 14-inch MacBook Pro with the standard M6 chip in October 2026. However, unlike previous generations, the M6 isn’t expected to be joined by more powerful M6 Pro and M6 Max versions.
Apple currently offers three processor options across the MacBook Pro range: the standard M5 in the entry-level 14-inch model, and the more powerful M5 Pro and M5 Max in the 14-inch and 16-inch models. The standard M6 is expected to replace the M5 almost exactly a year after its October 2025 launch.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is preparing to announce the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro in late October, potentially ahead of its October 28 media event. The new model is expected to retain the existing design, with the faster processor providing the main upgrade.
The more substantial changes, including an OLED touchscreen and redesigned chassis, are reportedly reserved for premium MacBook Pro models that will continue to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. Rather than introducing M6 Pro and M6 Max processors, Apple is reportedly fast-tracking the M7 generation, with M7 Pro and M7 Max models expected in fall 2027. For more on the redesigned models arriving this year, see our touchscreen MacBook Pro guide.
That creates an unusual buying decision: choose the standard M6 MacBook Pro, opt for one of the redesigned touchscreen models with M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, or wait for the next generation of professional processors in 2027. Here’s what the latest reports suggest.


M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
October 27, 2026
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple will announce the M6 iMac on October 27, 2026.


When Apple holds events on Wednesdays, it increasingly does so following three days of announcements. OLED iPad mini today, M6 iMac and MacBook Pro on Tuesday and touch MacBook Pro on Wednesday would make sense.
— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 26, 2026





On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026 that will feature the touchscreen MacBook Pro, but could mention the M6 model. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple is planning to announce the M6 MacBook Pro on October 27, 2026. According to the report, the launch will include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press.
More recently, reports have pointed to a media experience in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28, a day after Gurman’s originally reported announcement date. Apple could still unveil the new MacBook Pro on October 27 before giving invited journalists an opportunity to see the hardware the following day. 
Then on Monday October 19, Apple’s Greg Joswiak posted on X to say: “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.”  Indicating that the MacBook Pro will be updated in the week of 26 October.  


Can’t wait to pro and tell next week. pic.twitter.com/3wUkxwq35i
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026





The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to launch alongside the first OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac, and an updated iPad mini. The new entry-level MacBook Pro is expected to retain its 14-inch display and existing design, with the M6 chip providing the main upgrade.
The late October announcement would fit Apple’s recent release pattern. The M5 MacBook Pro arrived in October 2025, while its predecessor launched in November 2024.
Of the five generations of MacBook Pro, five have been released in the October/November timeframe. The list below also demonstrates that Apple doesn’t always introduce the standard, Pro and Max versions of a chip generation together.  
M5 Pro & M5 Max MacBook Pro: March 2026
M5 MacBook Pro: October 2025
M4, M4 Pro & M4 Max MacBook Pro: November 2024
M3, M3 Pro & M3 Max MacBook Pro: November 2023
M2 Pro & M2 Max MacBook Pro: January 2023
M2 MacBook Pro: June 2022
M1 Pro & M1 Max MacBook Pro: October 2021
M1 MacBook Pro: November 2020
Following the October 27 or 28 announcement, Gurman has indicated that the new MacBook Pro will start shipping on November 6. Ongoing memory and storage chip shortages could still affect availability or delivery times. These supply constraints have already contributed to price increases across Apple’s Mac lineup.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details
Expected M6 specs:
Same 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU as in the existing M6 Mac mini
TSMC 2nm manufacturing process
Up to 170GB/s memory bandwidth
Improved AI processing with Neural Accelerators

				
					

				
			
The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing.

Apple




Apple has introduced the M6 chip in the Mac mini, giving us a clear idea of what to expect from the upcoming MacBook Pro. The M6 is Apple’s first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm manufacturing process, bringing improvements to CPU, GPU, and AI performance.
The M6 in the Mac mini features a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, up from the M5’s 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU. It also introduces Neural Accelerators in every GPU core and a dual 16-core Neural Engine, boosting performance in AI workloads. The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to benefit from the same architectural improvements, making it particularly appealing to users running AI-powered applications and local AI models.
The Mac mini also provides an indication of what to expect from memory bandwidth. Earlier rumors suggested the M6 could reach 200GB/s, but the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 170GB/s with 24GB or 32GB of unified memory. The 16GB configuration offers 153GB/s, matching the M5. This relatively modest increase could limit the performance gains delivered by the redesigned GPU.
Our analysis suggests that the additional GPU cores, higher clock speeds, and architectural improvements help the M6 deliver gains of 20 percent or more in 3D graphics performance. However, memory bandwidth limitations mean those gains aren’t as substantial as the additional processing power might suggest.
The MacBook Pro’s exact M6 specifications remain unconfirmed, but the Mac mini offers a useful preview of the chip’s capabilities. The key question is whether Apple will make further changes to the processor or memory configurations when it brings the M6 to the MacBook Pro.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features
Existing 14-inch design expected; no OLED or touchscreen
The M6 MacBook Pro is expected to retain the existing 14-inch design, with few changes beyond the processor upgrade. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the display, chassis, and other hardware are likely to remain substantially unchanged from the M5 MacBook Pro.
That means buyers shouldn’t expect an OLED display or touchscreen on the standard M6 model. Those features are reportedly reserved for Apple’s redesigned premium MacBook Pro models, which are also expected to debut on October 27.

				
					

				
			
The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design.

Foundry




How is the M6 MacBook Pro different from the touchscreen MacBook Pro?
Apple is reportedly preparing two very different MacBook Pro updates for October 27.
The standard 14-inch MacBook Pro will move from the M5 to the M6 processor while retaining its familiar design. It should appeal to buyers who want the newer chip but don’t need a redesigned laptop.
The higher-end MacBook Pro models, meanwhile, are expected to introduce an OLED touchscreen, a reportedly thinner and lighter chassis, and potentially an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout. Despite these upgrades, the redesigned models will reportedly use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than M6 Pro and M6 Max processors.
This reflects Apple’s reported decision to skip the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation and focus development resources on the M7 family, which is expected in 2027.
Although the standard M6 is a newer chip, the M5 Pro and M5 Max are designed for more demanding professional workloads, so buyers shouldn’t assume the M6 MacBook Pro will be the more powerful option. It’s a similar situation to the Mac mini lineup, where the standard model features the M6 chip while the higher-end configuration uses the M5 Pro. 
The choice could therefore come down to whether buyers prioritize the latest chip at a lower price or a more powerful MacBook Pro with a redesigned display and chassis.


						

							






FeatureM6 MacBook ProOLED touchscreen MacBook Pro

Expected announcementOctober 27, 2026October 27, 2026
ProcessorM6M5 Pro / M5 Max
Screen sizes14-inchPremium MacBook Pro sizes; expected 14- and 16-inch
DisplayExisting non-OLED displayOLED
TouchscreenNoYes
DesignExisting chassisThinner, lighter redesign
PriceFrom around $1,999Higher pricing expected

 






M6 MacBook Pro: Price
$1,999/£1,999 starting price possible
We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal.
During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.”
The existing M5 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999/£1,999, following the price increases introduced in June 2026, and the M6 could retain that starting price.
However, another price increase is possible. Ongoing memory and storage shortages continue to affect Apple’s manufacturing costs, and the company may need to pass some of those costs on to buyers.
The redesigned OLED touchscreen models are also expected to carry a premium over the existing MacBook Pro lineup, making the standard M6 a potentially more affordable alternative for buyers who want a new MacBook Pro without paying extra for the redesigned display and chassis.


						

							


Should you wait for the M6 MacBook Pro?
With Apple’s next MacBook Pro announcement reportedly just days away, there’s a strong argument for waiting before buying a new 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Waiting until the end of October should provide a clearer picture of the M6 MacBook Pro’s performance, pricing, and availability, while potentially bringing discounts on the outgoing M5 model.
Wait for the M6 MacBook Pro if: You’re planning to buy the standard 14-inch MacBook Pro and don’t urgently need a new laptop. The M6 should provide improved CPU, GPU, and AI performance over the M5, without requiring a move to Apple’s more expensive Pro and Max models.
Consider the OLED touchscreen MacBook Pro if: You’re interested in a more substantial upgrade, particularly the rumored touchscreen display, OLED technology, and thinner design. Those models are expected to continue using M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, making them potentially better choices for demanding professional workloads.
Buy an M5 MacBook Pro now if: You need a laptop immediately or find a substantial discount. The existing M5, M5 Pro, and M5 Max MacBook Pro models remain capable machines, and a reduced price could make them better value than a newly launched M6 model.
Wait for the M7 MacBook Pro if: You’re particularly interested in OLED but don’t need the touchscreen. Reports suggest Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro could adopt the redesigned OLED chassis in 2027 with an M7 processor, although the timing remains uncertain.
For most people considering the entry-level MacBook Pro, waiting until October 27 makes sense. Even if the M6 doesn’t offer enough of an improvement to justify its price, its arrival could create opportunities to buy the outgoing M5 model at a discount.

title: Claude saves an overheating Mac from a cryptominer it might have put there
content:
Macworld





We’ve all heard about how AI is going to change the world as we know it. We’ve also heard about how AI can go rogue and do things that are, well, scary. These early days of AI development are filled with crazy stories, and since the Mac is popular amongs AI developers, you’ll hear a lot about them, especially if you’re a Mac enthusiast.
Take this recent story posted on Reddit by user UntilHEX, an AI developer whose Mac was consistently “running hot.” To identify the issue, they created an app using Claude Code to monitor their Mac’s temperature and identify the issue. During development, Claude ran a check on the accuracy of the Mac’s temperature sensor and discovered something that shouldn’t be there: a “cryptominer that I didn’t put there.”
That cryptominer caused temperature to spike to 112 degrees Celsius (233.6 degrees Farenheit) and CPU usage of 1175 percent. (With modern Macs, CPU usage is measured per core, so usage of over 100 percent is common.) Claude was able to trace the location of the cryptominer to a “LaunchAgents” folder that was put there “before I built anything.”
Despite Reddit users’ suspicions over Claude’s supposed innocence, it’s unclear exactly how the crypto malware was installed on the Mac. Claude offered to “clean it up” by quarantining the software in a folder, though UntilHEX had to manually remove one component because Claude didn’t have access to the part of macOS it needed. UntilHEX then ran a security check was done using a third-party app to make sure it was removed, and their Mac began to run normal again.

					
How to protect yourself from malware
This issue is unlikely to affect most users, but if you’re running AI agents, it’s a good idea to stay on track of your Mac’s vitals, which you can track in Activity Monitor. And if your agent has unfettered access to your Mac, it’s probably a good idea to keep a close eye on what it’s doing when you’re not around.
For everyone else, the easiest way to protect yourself from malware is to avoid downloading software from unfamiliar repositories. Apple has vetted software in the Mac App Store, and it is the safest way to get apps. If you prefer not to patronize the Mac App Store, then buy software directly from the developer and their website. If you insist on using cracked software, you will always risk malware exposure.
Never open links in emails or texts you receive from unknown and unexpected sources. If you get a message that looks like it is from an entity that you do business with, check the sender’s email address and inspect the URL carefully. If you see a link or button, you can Control-click it, select Copy Link Address, and then paste it into a text editor to see the actual URL and check it.
Macworld has several guides to help, including a guide on whether or not you need antivirus software, a list of Mac viruses, malware, and trojans, and comparison of Mac security software.

title: For the third time this fall, Apple prepares to launch a very cool thing nobody needs
content:
Macworld





Apple can’t win with people like me. When the company unveils minor iterative updates to successful products, we complain that it isn’t taking more risks. And when it launches crazy, beautiful tech in uncertain new markets, we suck our teeth and complain about practicality and necessity. It’s no wonder journalists are unpopular.
They’re damned if they do and they’re damned if they don’t. In which case, they might as well do whichever option is more fun–and Apple has spent this fall living that ethos to the max. First we got the iPhone Duo, a high-priced engineering wonder that nobody needs and everybody wants. Then we got the HomeView, the charming answer to a non-existent question. And now, unless every pundit on the planet has laid a gigantic predictive egg, we’re about to get a completely impractical and anti-ergonomic redesign of the MacBook for no other reason than it being cool.
Now, it isn’t surprising in the least that Apple’s senior management would have positive feelings about touchscreens, which were absolutely fundamental to the appeal and success of the iPhone (and later the iPad and Apple Watch) and are thus largely responsible for the company’s current wealth. But touchscreens are not the answer to every problem. They don’t work in every context.
Nobody suggests Apple should put a tiny touchscreen on the stem of your AirPods for the obvious reason that you wouldn’t be able to see it. Nobody thinks the Apple TV needs a touchscreen, or the HomePod a touchscreen that does anything more than turn it on and change the volume, because in both cases you’d have to get up and go over to the thing; far better to control it from your seat via a dedicated remote and your voice, respectively. But the MacBook, whose unsuitability for a touchscreen seems just as obvious to me, is in line to get one against all logic and reason.
The touchscreen on the iPhone works because you’re holding it. The device is held in a comfortable position for one hand, which (unless you have mismatched arms like the bodybuilder in Lady In The Water) automatically means it’s at a level and angle where it’s comfortable for the other arm to touch and interact with the screen. But the MacBook, with a few rare exceptions, is supported by either a desk or the user’s lap, which also supports your wrists while your hands use the keyboard and trackpad. Reaching up to touch the screen is an extra effort, tiring after virtually any time at all (just try it) and completely alien to the way laptops are used. I just don’t get the appeal at all.
And that’s just the physical, ergonomic side. There’s also the software aspect to consider: the way apps and the operating system would need to be reappraised for touch compatibility. Icons that are big enough to click are not necessarily big enough to tap, while design best practices for menus and buttons are drastically different in touch and non-touch contexts. Apple has up to now resisted the urge to combine macOS and iPadOS for good reason, which is that the two need to be different because they serve different needs. But if the MacBook gains a touchscreen display, macOS alone would need to serve both types of user interaction, which is a huge and unnecessary headache for the UX team, and likely users.
Ultimately, there are only two contexts in which a touchscreen MacBook makes any sense at all. One, proposed by my colleague Michael Simon in last week’s podcast, is that the product isn’t really a MacBook at all, but rather another new form factor for Apple: a laptop/tablet convertible. You’d only use the touchscreen when the keyboard is detached (or folded behind the screen), and it’s acting as a tablet; when it’s behaving as a laptop you’d revert to keyboard and trackpad. That could work, but I’m not convinced there’s a huge appetite for a touchscreen tablet with an optional keyboard when the iPad Pro and Magic Keyboard already exist and don’t exactly sell in earth-shattering quantities.
The other way it could work is to have touchscreen controls be 100 percent optional. Just build it as a normal MacBook that works exactly the way other MacBooks do, except that if you ever get the urge to touch the screen, like a confused toddler, then you can. Every now and then you’ll find a situation where the touchscreen option is better. Entering a digital signature, say, or selecting all the boxes containing a motorbike on a CAPTCHA test. The rest of the time, that entire facility may as well not be there.
Obviously that would be an eccentric approach to product design, to say the least. Upgrading a MacBook’s screen to support touch isn’t free, but rather requires a host of compromises and cost increases. Subjecting oneself to all that for the sake of a niche feature you’ll hardly ever use doesn’t seem like a very good idea. But at least it’s fun.

title: M6 iMac: Release date rumors, new colors, specs and price
content:
Macworld





Apple’s next iMac could be just days away. Nearly two years after the M4 iMac launched, Apple is reportedly preparing to introduce a new model powered by its M6 chip, potentially at the end of October 2026.
The good news is that the M6 promises a substantial performance upgrade, with a faster CPU and GPU, improved memory bandwidth and significant advances in AI processing. The less exciting news is that Apple isn’t expected to make major changes to the iMac’s design, although new colors could be on the way.
On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. This is expected to be the introduction of new Macs, including the M6 iMac.
Here’s everything we know about the M6 iMac, including its expected release date, design, specifications and price.
M6 iMac release date: When will it launch?
Expected release date: October 27, 2026
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple will announce the M6 iMac on October 27, 2026.


When Apple holds events on Wednesdays, it increasingly does so following three days of announcements. OLED iPad mini today, M6 iMac and MacBook Pro on Tuesday and touch MacBook Pro on Wednesday would make sense.
— Mark Gurman (@markgurman) October 26, 2026





On October 19, Apple announced a media event, dubbed “Pro and Tell” on October 28, 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman previously indicated that another Apple product launch was planned for Tuesday, October 27, so an announcement could still take place the day before the media gathering.
The M6 iMac is among the products expected to make an appearance, alongside new MacBook Pro M6 models, a touchscreen MacBook Pro, and an updated iPad mini. 
The prospect of an imminent iMac launch follows earlier reporting from Gurman. In the Q&A section of his August 23 Power On newsletter, Gurman indicated that the M6 iMac was close to launch and that customers should be able to buy one before the end of 2026.
An earlier July 2026 report also identified two iMac models, codenamed J833 and J834, among a wave of new Macs Apple was preparing.
The current M4 iMac arrived in fall 2024, making it nearly two years old. Apple appears to have skipped an M5 iMac altogether, as it previously skipped the M2 generation, meaning the next model should move directly from M4 to M6.
M6 iMac design: Will there be new colors?
Expected: The same 24-inch design, potentially with new color options.

				
					

				
			There are seven different colors available for iMac.
Apple




Anyone hoping for a completely redesigned iMac may be disappointed. According to Gurman’s August reporting, Apple is not preparing a major overhaul of its all-in-one desktop for 2026.
The iMac has retained essentially the same ultra-thin, colorful design since Apple introduced the 24-inch M1 iMac in 2021. Although the M4 iMac update in 2024 introduced some refinements, the overall appearance remained largely unchanged.
Gurman expects the M6 iMac to follow a similar pattern, with the new chip representing the most significant upgrade. However, he has suggested that new colors could be introduced.
Apple currently offers the iMac in seven colors: blue, green, pink, silver, yellow, orange and purple. These options have been available since 2021, although Apple refreshed the shades with the M4 model.
A more substantial iMac redesign could still arrive in a future generation, but there is currently little evidence to suggest that Apple is planning one for the M6 iMac.
M6 iMac display: Will it have a larger screen?

				
					

				
			Will Apple ever bring back the iMac Pro with a larger screen?
Foundry





Expected: A 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, similar to the current model.
The current model features a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, with a resolution of 4,480 by 2,520 pixels. It uses LED-backlit LCD technology and supports up to 500 nits of brightness. The M6 iMac is likely to retain a similar screen.
There have been rumors about Apple developing a larger iMac with more advanced display technology. In 2023, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo predicted a higher-end 32-inch iMac with a mini-LED display, potentially arriving in 2025. However, that product never materialized, and there is no reliable indication that it will launch alongside the M6 iMac.
M6 iMac specs and performance: How much faster will it be?
Expected: M6 chip, improved CPU and GPU performance, faster memory and a substantial AI upgrade.
The M6 iMac may not look very different from its predecessor, but the processor could make it a considerably more powerful computer.
Apple introduced the M6 chip in August 2026, with the new M6 Mac mini going on sale in September. That means we already have a useful indication of the technology the next iMac could include. You can read about how the Mac mini M6 chips compare to other Macs in our Best Mac guide. 
The M6 is Apple’s first chip manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, replacing the 3-nanometer technology used by the M4. The smaller manufacturing process allows Apple to improve transistor density, performance and power efficiency.
The M6 used in the Mac mini features:
A 12-core CPU.
A 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in every core.
A Dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI and machine-learning tasks.
16GB of standard unified memory, configurable up to 32GB.
Memory bandwidth of up to 170GB/s.
Improved storage performance compared with the M4 generation.
The M4 iMac currently offers an 8-core or 10-core CPU and an 8-core or 10-core GPU, depending on the configuration. Moving to the M6 could therefore bring a particularly noticeable performance improvement, especially for buyers upgrading from the entry-level M4 model.
Apple claims that the M6 Mac mini delivers up to 40 percent faster CPU performance, twice the graphics performance and four times the AI performance of the M4 Mac mini in its specified tests.
We can’t assume that the M6 iMac will achieve identical results, but these figures demonstrate the potential benefits of moving from the M4 to the M6 generation.
Improved AI performance
One of the biggest improvements could be the M6’s new AI-processing architecture.
Previous M-series chips used a single 16-core Neural Engine. The M6 introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, supported by Neural Accelerators in each GPU core.
Together, these changes should make the M6 iMac significantly better equipped for demanding AI workloads, including running local language models, processing images and using AI-powered creative tools.
For everyday users, the benefits may be less immediately obvious. However, the additional processing capabilities could become increasingly useful as macOS and third-party applications adopt more sophisticated on-device AI features.
More memory and faster connectivity
The M6 supports up to 32GB of unified memory and memory bandwidth of 170GB/s. Whether Apple offers the same memory configurations in the iMac remains to be seen.
The new Mac mini also includes Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, so these connectivity improvements seem likely to arrive on the M6 iMac as well.
It’s unknown if Apple will update the iMac’s Thunderbolt ports, storage options or other hardware features.
M6 iMac price: How much will it cost?
Expected starting price: Around $1,499.
When Apple introduced the M4 iMac in 2024, prices started at $1,299 for the entry-level model with an 8-core CPU, 8-core GPU and 256GB of storage. The higher-end version, featuring a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU, started at $1,499.
However, Apple increased the prices of the M4 iMac in June 2026. The entry-level model now starts at $1,499, while the four-port version starts at $1,699.
These price increases make it difficult to predict what Apple will charge for the next generation.
Apple could retain the current starting prices, particularly if the M6 update introduces relatively few changes beyond the processor. Alternatively, the higher cost of components and memory could result in further increases.
For now, $1,499 is a reasonable starting point for expectations.
Should you buy an M4 iMac or wait for the M6?
Our recommendation: Wait for the M6 iMac if you can.
With the next iMac potentially arriving before the end of October, we’d recommend holding off on buying the M4 model at full price.
The current iMac remains an excellent all-in-one desktop for everyday computing, home working, students and families. Its 24-inch Retina display, compact design and M4 processor make it more than capable of handling most people’s needs.
However, the M6 looks set to bring a meaningful increase in performance. The move from M4 to M6 should provide improvements to CPU and GPU performance, while the upgraded Neural Engine could make a difference as AI features become more demanding.
Waiting will also allow you to compare the new iMac’s pricing and specifications with those of the outgoing model. Even if you ultimately choose an M4 iMac, its replacement could make discounted older models more appealing.
There are reasons to buy now. If you need a new Mac immediately and find a substantial discount on an M4 iMac, it could still be a sensible purchase. But for anyone buying a new iMac at full price, waiting for Apple’s next announcement is the better option.

title: Apple Display Veterans Step Back as New Leaders Take Over
content:
Two executives who have spent roughly three decades each at Apple are handing over responsibility for its displays, as part of a broader series of engineering leadership changes reported by Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


Victor Yin now oversees much of Apple's display development following years of preparation under Wei Chen and John Zhong. title: Apple Addresses Web Security Threat, Working on macOS Update With Additional Fix
content:
Earlier this month, a security researcher discovered that private cryptographic keys associated with eight of Indian company eMudhra's intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates were weak. The compromised keys could have allowed attackers to impersonate legitimate websites, potentially putting users' sensitive information at risk. However, there is currently no evidence that the keys were exploited maliciously.


eMudhra's certificates were widely trusted by all major web browsers, including Safari, Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, but Apple and the other companies behind those browsers have since taken action to protect users.

support document, Apple said it has been blocking eMudhra's compromised TLS web certificates since October 19 in Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple's networking and security frameworks. The certificates are blocked automatically with no software update required, so most Apple device owners do not need to take any action.

There is one exception. Apple said those who use macOS command-line tools, such as system administrators, should be aware that some of those tools can still accept the compromised certificates until Apple releases a macOS update with a fix. In the meantime, Apple said those who use command-line tools can remove root CA certificates from the /etc/ssl/cert.pem file.

Apple has not provided a release date for the macOS update that will include the necessary changes to the /etc/ssl/cert.pem file by default.

title: Adjust iPhone Duo's Outer Display to Accommodate Your Case
content:
On iPhone Duo, Apple includes a display setting for cases or frames that partially cover the left edge of the outer display. It's called Shift Left Edge, and it insets the display edge so that on-screen content isn't hidden beneath the case. 


We first covered the setting in September, and Apple has since documented it, revealing that when you fit Apple's official iPhone Duo Case, a prompt automatically appears on the display to direct you to the setting. However, you can also turn it on manually at any time for third-party cases.

How to Turn On Shift Left Edge


Open the Settings app on your iPhone Duo.

Tap Display & Brightness.

Toggle on Shift Left Edge, then tap Enable in the prompt that appears.


The final prompt will tell you that your iPhone Duo needs to restart to apply the setting, but it's not a full reboot, and you'll be returned to the same settings screen after a brief black screen. 


If you subsequently swipe up to the Home Screen, you'll notice a narrow black border on the left side of the outer screen to accommodate the front portion of the case, leaving no content obscured.

title: iFixit iPhone Duo Teardown Points to Possible Cause of Screen Cracks
content:
Teardown site iFixit took apart the iPhone Duo to see what's inside, how it holds up to dust, and how repairable it is. There's a video walking through the teardown, as well as a blog post summing it up.



Before opening up the Duo, iFixit inundated it with fluorescent dust. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has an IP68 dust and water resistance rating, which means it's sealed against dust. iFixit found dust in the USB-C port, speaker mesh, and bezel, but few particles reached the internals of the device.

also did a dust test where particles entered the hinge and caused the magnets that hold the phone shut to fail.


iFixit was able to peel the cover layer away easily, which is as Apple intended. Apple made the nano-texture cover layer simple to remove so it could be replaced inexpensively, but you're not supposed to take it off on your own. With AppleCare+, replacing the cover layer is $19, and it's $49 without it.

iPhone 16, so a small electrical charge loosens the adhesive and allows the batteries to be removed. iFixit said it was the "best battery removal experience" from a foldable to date.


The outer display was easy to take off, and iFixit said the construction is "robust," which is a plus for repairability since most internal repairs have to go through the outer display. The inner screen trim comes off with heat, but there is a lot of adhesive to get through to remove the inner panel.

Apple describes the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s inner display as a 10-layer stack, and iFixit was able to peel back some of the layers to get a look at them under the microscope.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ uses an unstacked logic board, and it's the first iPhone to do so since the iPhone 8. The single-layer design is one way Apple kept the Duo thin.

some of the display failures people have been seeing, suggesting they could be caused by pressure, a trapped particle, repeated bending, or a manufacturing defect. It may not be that the display has physically snapped, because a wiring problem can cause the same effect.

Where most of the faulty units are experiencing issues, the hinge has a different shape. The failure spot is also near where the accordion cable passes by and where several edges meet, which could be leading to a concentration of stress in that spot. From iFixit:
To see where the stresses build up from folding, we built a 3D hinge model from teardown footage, patents, and CT scans, then compared it with the reported damage locations. The breaks cluster near the transition from the gap for the crossing flex cable to the central hinge support. The damage we're seeing in photos isn't right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends.

iFixit said it could also be the curved rails of the hinge that follow the screen's pivot points. The curved rails may be lifting above the flat plates of the hinge as the phone closes, and one rail lines up with the damage. It's possible a hinge component that's meant to retract isn't doing so, but there's no clear answer. The site has an interactive CT scan of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s hinge that shows how the supports, cable, and components fit beneath the display for anyone who wants to take a look.

With a repair manual available on day one, an option to remove the outer display intact, and batteries that release with an electrical charge, iFixit gave the ‌iPhone Duo‌ a provisional repair score of 5 out of 10. The inner display and hinge assembly are the biggest vulnerabilities, which cost the Duo points. "This is the most repairable foldable smartphone we've seen so far, and it's still going to be a bear to repair," said iFixit.
